questions: Did the facial weakness come on suddenly over hours to a few days?
Did the weakness begin on one side of your face before affecting the other?
Does the facial weakness worsen with sustained activity (like talking or chewing) and improve with rest?
Are you having difficulty chewing solid food?
Are you having trouble swallowing, or do foods or liquids go down the wrong way?
Have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs?
Have you experienced double vision?
Have you noticed any drooping of your eyelids?
Did you have a respiratory infection (such as a cold or flu) or diarrhea in the weeks before this started?
Have you developed a rash anywhere on your body?
Do you have any family members with similar facial weakness or muscle disease?
Has the weakness been getting progressively worse over weeks to months?
Have you had this problem for many years, slowly getting worse?
Have you noticed any change in your hearing or sense of taste?
Have you noticed dryness in your eyes or mouth?
Has your voice become more nasal-sounding?
Have you been exposed to ticks or spent time in wooded or grassy areas recently?
Do you have a history of autoimmune disease (such as thyroid disease or lupus)?
Do you have difficulty fully closing your eyes when you sleep?
Have you noticed any tremor, slowness of movement, or stiffness in your limbs?

Assess fatigability by asking her to sustain an upward gaze for 60 seconds.
Test for proximal limb weakness (shoulder abduction and hip flexion) against resistance.
Check deep tendon reflexes (biceps, triceps, knee, ankle) and for a jaw jerk.
Examine the tongue for wasting and fasciculations.
MRI of the brain (with thin cuts through the pons) to look for structural brainstem pathology.
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the facial muscles and a proximal limb muscle.
